senses: to choke, throttle, strangle (replaced in Classical Latin by suffoco)
to cause physical pain, to hurt
to cause mental pain, to distress, torment, torture, trouble, agitate, vex
to be tortured, grieved by, afflicted by
la:verb:ango.html:
ango, xi, ctum, and anxum, 3, v. a. (
perf. and sup. rest only on the assertion in P.; P.; part. anctus, Paul. ex Müll.; acc. to Prisc. l. c., the sup. is sometimes anxum; cf. Struve, 214) [the root of this word is widely diffused: ἄγκος, a bend, hollow; whence, valley, ravine; from the notion of closeness, come ἄγχω = to press tight, to strangle, throttle; ango; Germ. hangen, hängen; Engl. hang; angustus, anxius, anxietas; old Germ. Angust; Germ. Angst = Engl. anguish; from the notion of being bent, come ancus anculus, a crouching slave, ancora = Gr. ἄγκυρα; angulus = Germ. Angel, Engl. angle; old Germ. Angul, a hook; Gael. ingle = nook for the fire, fireplace; ancale = ἀγκάλη, Engl. ankle; ancon, and the pr. names Ancon and Ancona; uncus, curved, crooked; ungula, claw; unguis, claw, nail; cf. Sanscr. ahus, close; ahas, anguish; ankāmi, to bend; ankas, the lap (sinus), a hook; for the other Greek words belonging to this group, v. L. and S. s. vv. ἄγκος and ἄγχω].
Lit., to bind, draw, or press together; of the throat, to throttle, strangle (so ἄγχω; in this signif. antiquated; hence, in class. perh. only in the poets; in prose, instead of it, suffocare; cf. P.): angit inhaerens Elisos oculos et siccum sanguine guttur,; so : cum colla minantia monstri Angeret,; ; .—Hence, of plants, to choke, ; —
Metaph.
To cause (physical) pain; hence, angi, to feel or suffer pain, . —
Most freq. of the mind, to distress, torment, torture, vex, trouble; and angi, to feel distressed, to suffer torment, etc.: illum incommodis dictis angam,: cura angit hominem, * ; * : cruciatu timoris angi?: multa sunt, quae me sollicitant anguntque,: angebar singularum horarum exspectatio ne, et saep.; ; : ne munere te parvo beet aut incommodus angat (cruciet, cum non vult dare quod poscis, Cruqu.),: ad humum maerore gravi deducit et angit,: poëta, meum qui pectus inaniter angit,puts in torturing suspense,: Pompeius ... curis animum mordacibus angit,: Ea res animum illius anxit,: (aemula eam) vehementer angebat,.—With de (in respect to): de Statio manumisso et non nullis aliis rebus angor,: de quo angor et crucior,.—Sometimes with gen. (on this const. cf. Roby, II. § 1321): absurde facis, qui angas te animi,: (Sthenius) angebatur animi necessario, quod etc.,. But Cic. also uses the abl.: angor animo,: audio te animo angi, Fam. 16, 142; and acc. to some edd. Tusc. 1, 40, 96 Seyff. (v. further on this gen. s. v. animus).
la:verb:ango.inflection: xi, ctum, and anxum, 3, v. a.

la:adj:angustus.gloss: narrow, close, contracted, constricted, confined, small, not spacious
senses: narrow, close, contracted, constricted, confined, small, not spacious
la:adj:angustus.html:
angustus, a, um. adj.
v. ango
,
narrow, strait, esp. of local relations, close, contracted, small, not spacious (syn.: artus, brevis, contractus; opp. latus,).

Lit.: fretus,: Angustum per iter,; so , and ; : pontes angusti,: domus,: fauces portūs angustissimae,: fines, Herz.: cellae,: rima,: Principis angustā Caprearum in rupe sedentis,on the narrow rock, Herm., where Jahn reads augusta, both readings yielding an apposite sense: porta,; —Subst.: angustum, i, n., narrowness: per angustum,: angusta viarum,: pontes et viarum angusta,.—
Trop.
In angustum concludere, adducere, deducere, etc., to reduce to a strait, i. e. to restrain, confine, etc.: ab illā immensā societate humani generis in exiguum angustumque concluditur,: amicitia ex infinitā societate generis humani ita contracta est et adducta in angustum, ut, etc.,.—Of the passions, to curb, restrain, moderate: perturbationes animi contrahere et in angustum deducere,.—
Of other things: clavus angustus, the narrow purple stripe upon the tunic, v. clavus: spiritus,short, difficult,: odor rosae,not diffused far,.—Once also of the point of an arrow = acutus, , n. 2.—
Of time, short, brief: angustus dies,; : nox,: tempus,.—
Of means of living, and the like, pinching, scanty, needy: pauperies,: res angusta domi,: mensa,: domus, poor, i. e. built without much expense, .—
Of other external relations of life, difficult, critical, uncertain: rebus angustis animosus atque Fortis adpare,: cum fides totā Italiā esset angustior,was weakened,.—Subst.: angustum, i, n., a difficult, critical, condition, danger: in angustum cogi, * : res est in angusto,the condition is perilous,: spes est in angusto,hope is feeble,.—
Of mind or character, narrow, base, low, mean-spirited: nihil est tam angusti animi, tam parvi, quam amare divitias,: animi angusti et demissi,: ecce autem alii minuti et angusti, aut omnia semper desperantes, aut malevoli, invidi, etc.,.—
Of learned investigations that lay too much stress upon little things, subtle, hair-splitting: minutae angustaeque concertationes,: pungunt (Stoici) quasi aculeis, interrogatiunculis angustis,.—
Of discourse, brief, simple: et angusta quaedam et concisa, et alia est dilatata et fusa oratio,: Intonet angusto pectore Callimachus,i.e. in simple style,.—Adv.: angustē.
Lit., of space, quantity, or number, within narrow limits, closely, hardly: recepissem te, nisi anguste sederem, if I were not in close quarters, Cic. ap. : anguste putare vitem,to prune close,; so, anguste aliquid deputare,: quā (re frumentariā) anguste utebatur,in small quantity,: tantum navium repperit, ut anguste quindecim milia militum, quingentos equites transportare possent, = vix,scarcely fifteen thousand,.—Comp.: angustius pabulabantur,within narrower range,: aliae (arbores) radices angustius diffundunt,: quanto sit angustius imperitatum,: eo anno frumentum propter siccitates angustius provenerat,more scantily,.—Sup.: Caesar (nitebatur) ut quam angustissime Pompeium contineret,: furunculus angustissime praecisus,. —
Trop.
In gen., within narrow limits: anguste intraque civiles actiones coërcere rhetoricam,.— Comp.: haud scio an recte ea virtus frugalitas appellari possit, quod angustius apud Graecos valet, qui frugi homines χρησίμους appellant, id est tantum modo utiles, has a narrower meaning, : Reliqui habere se videntur angustius, enatant tamen etc.,seem to be more hampered,.—
Esp. of speaking or writing, closely, briefly, concisely, without diffuseness: anguste scribere, : anguste et exiliter dicere,: anguste disserere,: presse et anguste rem definire,: anguste materiem terminare,.—Comp.: Pergit idem et urget angustius,: concludere brevius angustiusque,.

la:noun:anguis.html:
anguis (dissyl.), is (rare form an-guen, like sanguen for sanguis, Mai.—
Abl. angue; but angui, Enn. ap. , or Trag. v. 51 Vahl.; ; MS.; cf. P.; in , suspected by Schne, on account of angue just before; angue also, Enn. ap. Acron. ad , or Trag. v. 441 Vahl.; Varr. Atac. ap. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 218), m. and f.; cf. P.; Rudd. I. p. 25; Neue, Formenl. I. p. 612 [cf. ἔγχελυς; Lith. angis; old Germ. unc = adder; ἔχις; ἔχιδνα = adder; Sanscr. ahis; Germ. Aal = Engl. eel. Curtius], a serpent, a snake (syn.: serpens, coluber, draco).
Lit.: angues jugati, Naev. ap. ; : emissio feminae anguis ... maris anguis,: vertatur Cadmus in anguem,—As fem.: caerulea, Enn. ap. : angues volucres vento invectae,: torta, Varr. Atac. ap. ; —Masc.: domi vectem circumjectus,: ater,: tortus,, and ; .—Sometimes serpent, snake, as a hateful, odious object: odisse aliquem aeque atque angues,: cane pejus et angui,.—
Transf.
In fable, an emblem.
Of terror; hence the snaky head of Medusa,.—
Of rage; hence the serpent-girdle of Tisiphone, and 511; her hair of snakes,; .—
Of art and wisdom; hence the serpent-team of Medea,, and of the inventive Ceres, ; cf. Voss, Mythol. Br. 2, 55.—
As a constellation.
= draco, the Dragon, between the Great and the Little Bear, ; : flexu sinuoso elabitur Anguis,: neu te tortum declinet ad Anguem,.—
= hydra, the Hydra, water-serpent, which extends over the constellations Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, carries on its back the Crater, and on its tail the Corvus, ; ; cf. .—
The Serpent, which Anguitenens (Ὀφιοῦχος) carries in his hand, .—
Prov.: Latet anguis in herbā, there's a snake in the grass, of some concealed danger, .

la:noun:angulus.html:
angŭlus, i, m.
cf. ἀγκύλος, crooked, bent, angular, Paul. ex Müll.; v. ango
,
an angle, a corner.
Lit.
Math. t. t., an angle: angulus optusus,: angulus acutus,: meridianus circulus horizonta rectis angulis secat,; so, ad pares angulos ad terram ferri,at right angles, perpendicularly,: Hoc ubi suffugit sensum simul angulus omnis,: figura, quae nihil habet incisum angulis, nihil anfractibus,.—
A corner: hujus lateris alter angulus qui est ad Cantium,: extremus,the extreme point, corner,; ; : arcae anguli,: quattuor anguli pallii,: hic factus est in caput anguli,the corner-stone,: anguli oculorum,the corners of the eyes,; : anguli parietum,the angles of walls,; so, murorum,: in angulis platearum,: quattuor anguli terrae,the four quarters of the earth,.—
Transf.
A retired, unfrequented place, a nook, corner, lurking-place: in angulum abire, * : nemo non modo Romae, sed nec ullo in angulo totius Italiae oppressus aere alieno fuit, quem etc.,: ille terrarum mihi praeter omnes Angulus ridet,: angulus hic mundi nunc me accipit,: gratus puellae risus ab angulo,; .—Contemptuously, of the schools or places of private discussion, in contrast with public, practical life: quibus ego, ut de his rebus in angulis consumendi otii causā disserant, cum concessero, etc.,: earum ipsarum rerum, quas isti in angulis personant, reapse, non oratione perfectio,; .—On the contr. without contempt, in Seneca, Ep. 95.—So also, detractingly, of a little country-seat, in opp. to the city: quod Angulus iste feret piper, that hole, said by the discontented steward, (so without detraction: recessus,).—* Trop.: me ex hoc, ut ita dicam, campo aequitatis ad istas verborum angustias et ad omnes litterarum angulos revocas, into every strait, embarrassment (the figure is taken from a contest or game, in which one strives to get his antagonist into a corner), .—
A projection of the sea into the land, a bay, gulf: Gallicus, Cato ap. P.

angor, ōris, m.
ango
, = angina.
A compression of the neck, a strangling: occupat fauces earum angor,the quinsy,: aestu et angore vexata, i.e. aestu angorem ac prope suffocationem efficiente,.—Far oftener,
Trop., anguish, torment, trouble, vexation (as a momentary feeling; while anxietas denotes a permanent state): est aliud iracundum esse, aliud iratum, ut differt anxietas ab angore; neque enim omnes anxii, qui anguntur aliquando; nec qui anxii, semper anguntur, etc.,: angor est aegritudo premens,; : anxius angor,; so : animus omni liber curā et angore,: angor pro amico saepe capiendus,; : angor animi,; so al.—In plur.: confici angoribus,; .
